text: Room opened — goal: improve: Self-improvement: review prompts/engines/routing/own-code; auto-apply safe changes; pitch

name: Sprocket
text: Add a "safe-change" flag to every prompt that lets us auto-apply edits when the diff is under 10 lines and passes a quick syntax check. This cuts review time for trivial fixes without risking big rewrites. The trade-off is we might miss subtle context shifts in longer edits, so we keep the flag off by default and log every auto-apply for later spot-checks.

name: Gauge
text: The "safe-change" flag risks normalizing sloppy edits—10 lines is arbitrary, and syntax checks miss semantic drift. Better: auto-apply only when the diff is a single-line tweak *and* the change is a known safe pattern (e.g., typo fixes, doc updates). Settle it by running a 2-week trial on non-critical files and measuring how often auto-applied changes require rollback.

name: Sprocket
text:
Add a "single-line safe-change" flag that auto-applies only typo fixes, doc updates, and one-line tweaks matching a curated list of safe patterns. This cuts review time for the most common trivial edits without risking bigger rewrites. The trade-off is we’ll reject some valid but unlisted safe changes, but the strict whitelist keeps semantic drift near zero.

name: Gauge
text: The "single-line safe-change" flag still risks missing context shifts—typos in docstrings can break API contracts, and one-line tweaks might violate implicit team conventions. Better: auto-apply only edits that match a pre-approved, machine-readable rule set (e.g., "fix spelling in comments," "update copyright year") with a strict allowlist. Settle it by running a 2-week trial on non-critical files and measuring the error rate—if it exceeds 0.1%, kill the flag.

name: Ratchet
text: DECISION: Auto-apply only edits matching pre-approved, machine-readable rules (e.g., "fix spelling in comments," "update version in changelog")—no flags, no exceptions. Result: a curated rule set and a bot that enforces it. Owner: Gauge.
